title: Morning Edition
dek: Ukraine's aid-shelter toll rises; North Korea tests missiles; a carbon-storage proposal; and the end of a space telescope's long watch.

lead_story.headline: Death toll rises to 42 after Russian strike on Ukrainian aid shelter
lead_story.summary: Ukrainian police say 42 people have died after Russian bombs hit a school used as a shelter and aid distribution site in Komyshuvakha. Reuters verified police body-camera footage showing events before a second strike; rescue workers continue searching the rubble. Russia says it targeted military units.
lead_story.why_it_matters: The reported civilian toll and documented sequence raise urgent questions about civilian protection as US-brokered talks approach. The competing military claims are not independently resolved.

items.headline: North Korea reports new air-defence test and cruise-missile drill
items.summary: North Korean state media says the military tested an air-defence missile and simulated an airport strike with cruise missiles. South Korea independently detected multiple launches; the performance claims remain Pyongyang's.
items.why_it_matters: The launches sharpen regional security concerns, but official weapons-test claims should not be confused with independently demonstrated capabilities.

items.headline: Australia designates offshore site for proposed Japanese carbon storage
items.summary: Australia has designated seabed near Darwin for a possible carbon capture and storage project led by Japan's Inpex. Further environmental approvals and licenses are required before injection can begin.
items.why_it_matters: The project illustrates a contested climate tradeoff: reducing industrial emissions versus prolonging gas extraction and disturbing marine habitat.

items.headline: NASA's Swift telescope returns to Earth after 22 years
items.summary: The Swift Observatory reentered near Indonesia after operating about eleven times longer than its planned two-year mission. A proposed robotic orbit-raising rescue failed; Swift had helped scientists study thousands of gamma-ray bursts.
items.why_it_matters: The loss closes a productive astronomy mission and highlights the growing importance of orbital maintenance for aging observatories.

items.headline: Big Tech rallies while data-centre operators fall after US midterms
items.summary: Markets diverged after Democratic congressional victories: major technology firms gained as some investors anticipated slower data-centre expansion, while specialist infrastructure stocks fell. The explanation is analysts' interpretation, not a proven causal forecast.
items.why_it_matters: The split reveals how constraints on new computing capacity might benefit incumbents while hurting debt-financed builders.

items.headline: Older catch-up: a Gabonese plant enters a debate over medicinal promise and cultural rights
items.summary: Reporting from Gabon examines iboga, a plant important to Bwiti traditions and studied for possible addiction treatment, as overseas commercial interest grows. Clinical efficacy, safety and sustainable sourcing remain unsettled.
items.why_it_matters: The story links medical research to questions of Indigenous knowledge, consent, conservation and who benefits from commercialization.

items.headline: Mooresville prepares its fiftieth Working Fingers craft show
items.summary: The town's annual handmade-goods fair is scheduled for November 7 at the Charles Mack Citizen Center. Organizers describe free entry and stalls featuring jewelry, art, clothing and baked goods; it is an upcoming event, not a report that it already occurred.
items.why_it_matters: A small local tradition shows the ordinary social life of makers and neighbors beyond the national news cycle.

items.headline: Intellectual humility is not always the virtue we think it is
items.summary: Philosopher Rachel Fraser argues that intellectual traits such as confidence and humility cannot be labeled universally virtuous: their usefulness depends on context, evidence and the work at hand. Barbara McClintock's scientific persistence offers a case.
items.why_it_matters: The argument complicates easy advice to always be humble and asks what intellectual habits actually help us find truth.

worth_your_time.headline: Can making medicines in orbit ever make economic sense?
worth_your_time.summary: A reported feature examines Varda's drug-crystal experiments in microgravity and other startups' ambitions for space manufacturing. Researchers see possible advantages for some materials, but commercial scale, costs and regulation remain unresolved.
worth_your_time.why_it_matters: The story offers a concrete way to judge space-industry promises: repeatable product improvements must outweigh launch, recovery and quality-control costs.

daily_wonder.title: A naturalist's geometry of jellyfish
daily_wonder.caption: Ernst Haeckel's 1904 plate from Kunstformen der Natur arranges several discomedusan jellyfish as a study in symmetry, anatomy and variation. It is a scientific illustration, not a photograph or a modern taxonomic chart.
daily_wonder.alt: Vintage natural-history illustration with several blue, gold and reddish jellyfish arranged symmetrically against a light background.
daily_wonder.credit: Ernst Haeckel; scan Ragesoss; cleanup Ilmari Karonen; Wikimedia Commons
daily_wonder.rights: Public domain (1904 publication; author died 1919), Public Domain Mark 1.0

reflection.passage: I am a part of all that I have met;
reflection.author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
reflection.context: Tennyson's dramatic speaker is an aging Ulysses who sees his identity as shaped by encounters and travel. The poem's restless appetite for further experience can be inspiring, but it also raises questions about his duties to those he leaves behind.
reflection.question: Which encounters have changed how you understand yourself?
